questions.q: What does the article mean by “one man, two missions”?
options: Following two religions
Not quite. The article says: Dividing one’s life consciously between earning a lawful livelihood and serving its higher purpose.
Dividing one’s life consciously between earning a lawful livelihood and serving its higher purpose
Yes. Neither neglecting the world nor being enslaved to it.
Working for two employers
Not quite. The article says: Dividing one’s life consciously between earning a lawful livelihood and serving its higher purpose.
Holding two jobs at once
Not quite. The article says: Dividing one’s life consciously between earning a lawful livelihood and serving its higher purpose.
questions.rationale: “A person divides his life between earning a lawful livelihood and pursuing the real purpose of his existence.”

questions.q: According to the article, what matters in the life to come?
options: Not how much one does, but what one becomes through what one does
Right. Deeds without inner change are barren.
The number of deeds performed
Not quite. The article says: Not how much one does, but what one becomes through what one does.
How busy one has been
Not quite. The article says: Not how much one does, but what one becomes through what one does.
How others have judged one’s work
Not quite. The article says: Not how much one does, but what one becomes through what one does.
questions.rationale: “What truly matters in the life to come is not how much one does, but what one becomes through what one does.”

questions.q: The article calls the cosmos “a moral classroom.” Which lesson does it draw from the stars?
options: They compete for space
Not quite. The article says: They keep to their orbits without colliding – man too should act within his limits and avoid needless conflict.
They keep to their orbits without colliding – man too should act within his limits and avoid needless conflict
Yes. Trees, likewise, teach returning good for evil.
They never change
Not quite. The article says: They keep to their orbits without colliding – man too should act within his limits and avoid needless conflict.
They shine brightest when alone
Not quite. The article says: They keep to their orbits without colliding – man too should act within his limits and avoid needless conflict.
questions.rationale: “Billions of stars move in precise orbits without colliding; man, too, is required to function within his own limits, avoiding unnecessary conflict.”

questions.q: Why does the article say a person has no moral right to waste his life?
options: Because life is very long
Not quite. The article says: He did not create it – it is a trust from God, for which he will be questioned.
Because society forbids it
Not quite. The article says: He did not create it – it is a trust from God, for which he will be questioned.
He did not create it – it is a trust from God, for which he will be questioned
Well read. Using it well is an act of gratitude.
Because others depend on him for money
Not quite. The article says: He did not create it – it is a trust from God, for which he will be questioned.
questions.rationale: “Life is not self-created. It is a trust given by the Lord of the universe. Since a human being cannot create life, he has no moral right to waste it.”

questions.q: What question does the successful person ask when difficulties come?
options: Not why they have come, but what they demand of him
Correct. Every challenge asks how we will respond.
Why others are spared
Not quite. The article says: Not why they have come, but what they demand of him.
How to escape them at once
Not quite. The article says: Not why they have come, but what they demand of him.
Who is to blame for them
Not quite. The article says: Not why they have come, but what they demand of him.
questions.rationale: “The successful person does not ask why difficulties come; he asks what they demand from him.”

questions.q: Alfred Nobel read his own mistaken obituary, which called him “the merchant of death.” How did he respond?
options: He built more factories
Not quite. The article says: With reflection, not anger – he left most of his wealth to found the Nobel Prizes.
With reflection, not anger – he left most of his wealth to found the Nobel Prizes
Yes. A shock became a turning point.
He withdrew from public life
Not quite. The article says: With reflection, not anger – he left most of his wealth to found the Nobel Prizes.
He sued the newspaper
Not quite. The article says: With reflection, not anger – he left most of his wealth to found the Nobel Prizes.
questions.rationale: “Instead of reacting with anger or denial, Nobel responded with reflection. In 1895, he signed his will, setting aside most of his wealth to establish the Nobel Prizes.”

questions.article: The World and Its Perfect Counterpart
questions.q: On what single basis, according to the article, will people be selected for the perfect world of the Hereafter?
options: Their wealth
Not quite. The article says: The right or wrong use of the freedom they were given.
The length of their lives
Not quite. The article says: The right or wrong use of the freedom they were given.
The right or wrong use of the freedom they were given
Right. This world is a selection ground.
Their ancestry
Not quite. The article says: The right or wrong use of the freedom they were given.
questions.rationale: “There is only one criterion: the right or wrong use of the freedom granted to human beings.”

questions.q: How does the writer describe the relation between science and faith on what lies beyond death?
options: They contradict each other
Not quite. The article says: They complete one another – science observes the phenomenon, faith explains its meaning.
They complete one another – science observes the phenomenon, faith explains its meaning
Yes. “Science says life after death may be possible. Faith says it is certain.”
Science has replaced faith
Not quite. The article says: They complete one another – science observes the phenomenon, faith explains its meaning.
Neither has anything to say
Not quite. The article says: They complete one another – science observes the phenomenon, faith explains its meaning.
questions.rationale: “Science and faith are not in conflict; they complete one another. Science observes the phenomenon. Faith explains its meaning.”

questions.q: What does the article name as the decisive factor in Japan’s recovery after earthquake and war?
options: The will to act – choosing effort and reconstruction over despair and protest
Exactly. Not material abundance.
Help from neighbouring countries
Not quite. The article says: The will to act – choosing effort and reconstruction over despair and protest.
A long period of rest
Not quite. The article says: The will to act – choosing effort and reconstruction over despair and protest.
Rich natural resources
Not quite. The article says: The will to act – choosing effort and reconstruction over despair and protest.
questions.rationale: “The decisive factor in this remarkable recovery was not material abundance, but the will to act.”

questions.q: From what does the article say backbiting usually springs, and where does reform begin?
options: Inner insecurity and fear – so reform begins with building inner security through faith
Well reasoned. “Speak good or remain silent.”
Too much confidence – so reform begins with humility
Not quite. The article says: Inner insecurity and fear – so reform begins with building inner security through faith.
Lack of information – so reform begins with study
Not quite. The article says: Inner insecurity and fear – so reform begins with building inner security through faith.
Boredom – so reform begins with keeping busy
Not quite. The article says: Inner insecurity and fear – so reform begins with building inner security through faith.
questions.rationale: “Backbiting is rarely the act of a confident person. It is usually the act of someone who feels insecure… reform does not begin merely by controlling speech. It begins by building inner security.”
